To mitigate triangle counting on massive graphs, distributed-memory partitioned-graph approaches are viable (i.e., assessing closed wedges independently within a partition), but load imbalance due to arbitrary communication can overshadow any gains from enhanced concurrency, owing to the inherent lack of structure in regular graphs. In this paper, we discuss a distributed-memory exact graph triangle counting implementation, and assess its performance over billion-edge real-world graphs on contemporary scale-out and scale-up based NVIDIA GPU platforms (considering NVIDIA ``Ampere'' and ``Hopper'' architectures), depicting a scalability spectrum of multiple orders of magnitude. Comparisons with existing state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates up to 10$\times$ improvements relative to distributed-memory CPU baseline, 2-100$\times$ over single-GPU vendor-optimized NVIDIA RAPIDS cuGraph and 10-60\% over multi-GPU $G^2$Miner, in terms of end-to-end execution times.

title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
summary: Long contexts increase the memory cost of the key-value (KV) cache in large language model (LLM) inference. Sparse attention reduces attention computation and memory traffic by selecting historical tokens, but the retained KV cache must remain available for later decoding steps. We present UlaCache, a KV cache management system built around a unified logical address space spanning GPU KV pools and optional CPU memory. Stable logical references let the inference engine allocate and select KV independently of physical placement. Common allocation and sparse-access interfaces support data-parallel (DP) and tensor-parallel (TP) attention. For distributed storage, local GPU buffers retain selected KV across decoding steps, so only missing entries require transfers. When CPU storage is enabled, Parallel Bucketed LRU (PB-LRU) manages a GPU pool shared across requests. It updates recency metadata and selects eviction victims in parallel. UlaCache transfers KV and then updates the address mappings. With speculative decoding enabled under matched CPU and GPU memory budgets, UlaCache achieves peak decoding throughput speedups of 1.16 $\times$ (DP) and 1.70 $\times$ (TP) on H200, and 1.73 $\times$ (DP) and 2.51 $\times$ (TP) on B300, compared with the state-of-the-art baseline.

title: Prefix Visibility Ratio: Quantifying Partial Observability in Carpet Bombing Detection
summary: Carpet bombing attacks distribute malicious traffic across many destinations within a network prefix, while operational monitoring commonly provides destination-specific telemetry for only a subset of those targets. This creates an attack-conditional observability problem that is not captured by address utilization or nominal monitoring coverage. We introduce the Prefix Visibility Ratio (PVR), defined as the fraction of attacked destinations for which the telemetry required by the host-level evidence plane is available, and argue that PVR should be treated as an explicit evaluation dimension for carpet bombing detection. We then present VANTA (Visibility-Aware Network Threat Analysis) as one concrete way to operationalize this principle. VANTA combines host-level and prefix-level anomaly scores, estimates PVR online from router-side destination evidence and the monitored-destination inventory, and adjusts evidence fusion according to both estimated visibility and estimator confidence. Across a validated campaign of 2,160 Mininet runs, VANTA achieves 99.18% precision, 93.46% recall, a global F1-score of 96.24%, and a 1.54% false-positive rate. In a separate matched-observability study using task-adapted feature-level reference implementations, VANTA reaches 95.89% pooled F1 and 92.39% recall for configured PVR<=10%, with its largest advantage appearing at configured PVR=1%. These reference comparisons are intended to isolate observability effects under a common binary detection task rather than to reproduce the original end-to-end objectives of the referenced systems. The results establish attacked-destination visibility as a measurable factor that can materially change detector behavior and should be reported explicitly in future carpet bombing evaluations.

title: D-Pingmesh: Dynamic Probing and Fault Localization for Reconfigurable Datacenter Networks
summary: Pingmesh monitors datacenter networks through periodic pings between servers. In reconfigurable datacenter networks, topology engineering (TPE) and traffic engineering (TE) make uniform server-pair probing inefficient: a pinglist wastes budget retesting common paths while missing low-probability interfaces. Frequent control-plane updates further require rapid pinglist refresh, and cause path ambiguity at control-plane boundaries for fault localization. We present D-Pingmesh, a probing and fault-localization system co-designed with the TPE/TE control plane. Its control-plane-aware generator builds task-efficient pinglists by greedily admitting probes with high interface coverage under the current TPE/TE snapshot. An incremental replay-and-repair mechanism updates pinglists across reconfigurations rather than recomputing from scratch. At control-plane boundaries, a Rho-EM localizer jointly infers per-task old/new-path mixture weights and the fault set through EM-style iteration. We evaluate D-Pingmesh on an 8-pod reconfigurable topology under dynamic TPE/TE. At a 0.99 coverage target, D-Pingmesh uses 17.7x fewer tasks than Pingmesh and generates each pinglist about 5.1x faster than RD-Probe. In ns-3 simulation, boundary-aware localization improves micro F1 from 0.871 to 0.953 over the deTector PLL baseline. A testbed deployment demonstrates second-scale fault localization with low host overhead. These results demonstrate that D-Pingmesh is practical for reconfigurable datacenter networks with control-plane-aware monitoring.

title: Do Flow-Generation Tools Matter? Unsupervised Characterization of MQTT Traffic Across Public Datasets
summary: Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT) is widely used in IoT environments due to its lightweight publish-subscribe design and suitability for resource-constrained networks. While current MQTT security studies mainly focus on detecting attacks and optimizing classification performance, this work takes a different perspective by presenting a cross-dataset, tool-aware characterization of MQTT traffic at the flow level. This perspective is motivated by the fact that flow-generation is tool-dependent: flows are not directly observed in packet captures, but are constructed through tool-specific decisions about packet grouping, flow termination, and feature export. Using packet captures from 4 public MQTT datasets, we generated over 380K flows with 3 open-access flow-generation tools: Zeek-flowmeter, Argus, and NTLFlowLyzer. We analyzed the tool-specific flows using K-means, DBSCAN, and HDBSCAN, with and without PCA-based dimensionality reduction. We measured clustering quality using 2 metrics: (1) Silhouette score to assess label-independent cluster compactness and separation, and (2) Adjusted Rand Index to measure agreement with available labels. Our results show that the choice of flow-generation tool affects the resulting flow population, feature-space structure, and clustering behavior. Zeek-flowmeter achieves the best performance in several settings, particularly with K-means and PCA reduction to 10 components. Yet, no single tool consistently dominates across all datasets, algorithms, and evaluation metrics. These findings show that flow-level MQTT analysis should treat the dataset, flow-generation tool, preprocessing choices, clustering algorithm, and evaluation metric as interconnected experimental factors.

title: SAKURA: Serving Attention Key-Value State Under Rate Adaptation for Private Image Editing on Phones
summary: Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks. We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.

title: Through the Looking Glass: Analyzing Geolocation Providers Using Looking Glasses and Active Measurements
summary: Looking Glass servers (LGs) allow users and network operators to debug issues or measure performance to/from arbitrary, external IP addresses, making LGs a valuable tool in a variety of analyses. To assess the reliability of LGs as an independent and free set of vantage points, we perform an analysis of 4487 LG servers across 144 countries. We analyze LGs by comparing them to six different geolocation databases from four providers, and by conducting active measurements on LGs. In our RTT measurements we find 9 of 18 LG providers have at least one server with an RTT-disconfirmed location. We also find substantial differences between geolocation databases' ability to locate LGs, with IPinfo showing the closest distance to LGs.

title: A DIY DPDK Software Router for Networking Education
summary: High-performance packet processing frameworks, such as the Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK), are widely used in modern network systems, yet they are rarely integrated into networking curricula. As a result, students often lack exposure to the performance considerations and low-level design choices that shape real-world packet processing systems. We describe a semester-long course project in which students implement a do-it-yourself (DIY) software router using DPDK in a master-level computer networking course. The project guides students through the design and implementation of a multithreaded router, the development of a routing table data structure, and the evaluation of forwarding performance using standard benchmarking tools. We present the project structure and the virtualized infrastructure used to support classes of realistic size. Based on several iterations of the course and survey feedback from participating students, we discuss the observed workload, learning outcomes, and challenges of teaching high-performance packet processing. We release the project material and scripts to recreate the infrastructure, enabling reuse and further refinement by the community.

title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
summary: Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model--hardware co-design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low-bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split-channel large-kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier-free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in-domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute-array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic-array accelerator with 8-bit $\times$ 8-bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low-bit hardware.

title: Semantic-Aware Update Admission and Adaptive Byzantine Redundancy for Secure Computation Offloading in COIN-Enabled Metaverse Systems
summary: Computing in the network (COIN) supports latency-sensitive Metaverse services, but blockchain commitment of persistent shared-state updates competes with application execution for limited resources. We consider the joint problem of deciding which updates to commit, how much Byzantine redundancy to provision, and where to execute Metaverse application tasks. We formulate this problem under resource, latency, and practical Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT) constraints, accounting for update persistence and semantic significance. We develop a hierarchical redundancy-aware PBFT (R-PBFT) approach that decomposes the decision process into slot-wise computation offloading and sequential update-admission and redundancy control. We formulate the former as an identical-interest game and address the latter using a feasibility-filtered double deep Q-network (DDQN). Analytical downlink allocation accounts for the energy and delivery-feasibility effects of consensus latency. For fixed slot state and redundancy, we establish the game's exact-potential property and finite termination of strict sequential improvements. Feasible-action filtering enforces configured Byzantine redundancy and blockchain-budget constraints independently of learning. Numerical results show relative improvements of up to $46.7\%$ in reward averaged across tested user loads and seeds over Minimum Secure, the strongest baseline on average. At the highest tested Byzantine bound, the secure timely-update ratio improves by $62.3\%$ over the same baseline. Ablations assess the contributions of feasibility filtering and adaptive deferral.

title: RISK-KV: Quality-Aware Selective KV Cache Reconstruction for Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Request migration and interruption recovery in distributed large language model (LLM) inference rely on historical key-value (KV) caches. Retaining or transferring a complete cache incurs substantial state overhead, whereas replaying historical tokens requires additional computation. This paper proposes RISK-KV, a quality-aware method for selective historical KV reconstruction in pretrained models. RISK-KV uses exact KV states on both sides of a target layer and cross-layer ridge regression to predict the missing layer's attention-projection input; it then folds in the original model's KV projection matrices to reduce predictor storage. Reconstruction risk is measured by the change in negative log-likelihood (NLL) caused by actual reconstruction, and low-overhead topology search with quality gating selects the layer groups to reconstruct. Independent tests on three language models show that representative recovery configurations omit 18.2 percent to 33.3 percent of historical KV, with perplexity changes below 0.5 percent. In a local request-recovery experiment with a 512-token history, RISK-KV achieves a 1.51 to 3.31 times speedup over full Token Replay. These results indicate that selective KV reconstruction can reduce historical cache overhead with small changes in predictive quality and improve request-recovery efficiency under the evaluated deployment conditions.

title: Hard and Soft Real-Time DNN Inference Scheduling on Heterogeneous Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning
summary: We present a scheduling framework for heterogeneous multi-accelerator systems executing both hard real-time and soft real-time QoS-aware DNN inference workloads. The framework combines an online reinforcement learning (RL) scheduler with a deterministic runtime safety layer. The RL scheduler dynamically generates candidate schedules by jointly selecting sub-job priorities and accelerator assignments, while runtime certification guarantees that all HRT deadlines remain satisfied independently of the learned policy. To enable runtime certification in heterogeneous precedence-constrained systems, we introduce a schedulability-preserving prefix replacement criterion based on machine-wise cuts. The proposed criterion guarantees that runtime-generated schedule prefixes preserve the existence of a feasible continuation without requiring complete finish-time dominance with respect to a feasible reference schedule. Experimental results on heterogeneous DNN accelerator platforms show that the proposed framework preserves HRT schedulability while improving QoS-aware deadline satisfaction, client-level service quality, and accelerator utilization compared to state-of-the-art scheduling approaches.

title: How Not to Be Censored: Inclusion Safety in Client-Led Consensus
summary: Blockchain consensus protocols implicitly follow a client-server architecture: validators are the only active participants, while clients (i.e., users) merely submit transactions and rely on validators to include them. This abstraction obscures a fundamental question: what should a client do to guarantee the timely inclusion of its own transaction? We study this question by introducing a leaderless consensus protocol in which clients are active. We define inclusion safety: the guarantee that a client's transaction enters some of the blocks produced for an epoch, and that every block omitting it belongs to a fork that is eventually abandoned. Because every transaction carries a reference to a block of the previous epoch, clients help select the surviving fork. This yields two paths to inclusion: reaching sufficiently many honest replicas within an epoch, or relaying a block containing the transaction across epochs until the corresponding fork becomes canonical. In a generalized model spanning synchrony and asynchrony, the client's and the replicas' connectivity are substitutes for inclusion safety: it is achieved either if the client is well connected, or if the client is poorly connected but honest replicas communicate reliably, provided the client reaches at least one of them. However, the substitution is imperfect: when inclusion safety rests on the replicas' connectivity, it requires a longer epoch compared to when the client is well connected.

title: Reorienting the Vector Axis: Restructuring FlashAttention for Long-Vector Processors
summary: A Transformer is built around attention, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length and dominates the layer on long sequences. FlashAttention made that cost manageable by tiling the attention matrix and updating the softmax as it goes, but almost all work since has targeted GPUs. On long-vector processors one vector register can hold up to 512 single-precision numbers. The savings of a vector instruction are proportional to how much of the register it uses, so the choice of which loop to vectorize is a first-order decision. We port PyTorch's CPU FlashAttention kernel to a RISC-V CPU with 2KB vector registers and find that it reaches 16.2% of peak floating-point throughput. The kernel walks each tile one query row at a time: the product against V is vectorized along the 64-element head dimension, the softmax's per-row maximum and sum are reductions that collapse a full register to a scalar, and the software exponential's polynomial coefficients compete with tile data for vector registers and cause spilling. We propose two techniques. The first transposes the score tile and the running output so that queries lie along the contiguous axis. The algorithm and its values are unchanged. A single parameter, the number of queries in a tile, now sets the vector length of every part of the kernel and can be matched to the machine. Both reductions also disappear. The second moves the polynomial's coefficients into scalar registers, removing the spills and cutting the softmax's vector memory instructions by 78.7%. On silicon the two together cut whole-kernel cycles by 1.84 to 2.08x at a head dimension of 64, raising floating-point utilization from 16.2% to 29.7% of peak. An FPGA of the same design ranks the changes identically and scores them higher, at 2.71x.

title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
summary: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at $k=2$. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.

title: RadioDreamer: A World Model for Radio Map Forecasting and Imagination-Based Optimization
summary: Radio maps characterize the spatial distribution of wireless conditions and are fundamental to network planning and optimization. However, existing learning-based methods reconstruct isolated radio-map snapshots and do not model how network actions drive the evolution of the radio environment. In this paper, we present RadioDreamer, a two-stage world model that unifies action-conditioned radio-map forecasting and imagination-based network optimization within a latent space. To learn causal environmental transitions from sequential interactions, we introduce a structured spatio-temporal transformer backbone coupled with dynamic-region supervision, enabling accurate modeling of action-sensitive areas. Second, rather than relying on conventional physical trial-and-error, RadioDreamer establishes a general planning paradigm that generates counterfactual latent trajectories to evaluate and optimize long-horizon network parameter configurations. Experiments show that RadioDreamer improves both multi-step rollout forecasting and closed-loop network optimization. It reduces full-map forecasting error by 25.2% on average and achieves approximately 80% accuracy in predicting the evolution direction of radio signals. More importantly, for long-horizon network configuration, imagination-based planning surpasses model-free policies optimized directly on radio-map observations by 8.8% in accumulated return.

title: MASAR: Multi-stage Attack Surface Analysis and Reasoning Framework for Telecom Networks
summary: The increasing complexity of modern telecommunications networks introduces security challenges that require systematic threat analysis. However, a gap remains between architectural threat modeling frameworks, such as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege (STRIDE), and operational knowledge bases, such as the MITRE Five-G Hierarchy of Threats (FiGHT). This gap limits the ability to connect architectural weaknesses with specific protocol behaviors and attack sequences. This paper presents Multi-stage Attack Surface Analysis and Reasoning (MASAR), a formal framework that bridges this gap through three layers: strategic threat mapping, logical attack path decomposition using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and operational synthesis of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). MASAR is evaluated using a 5G-ready IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) architecture, examining two signaling attack scenarios: early media billing bypass through Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) signaling and subscriber information disclosure and topology discovery through the Diameter Cx interface. MiniZinc constraint models are used to analyze the reachability of unsafe protocol states. The analysis demonstrates how MASAR connects architectural threats with specific protocol behaviors and supports security controls that account for network states in telecommunications systems.

title: Workflow-Aware Communication and Computation Scheduling for Mobile Edge AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in mobile edge environments to autonomously handle diverse tasks through multi-step workflows. Unlike conventional dependency-aware tasks with predefined dependency structures, agent workflows are dynamically generated based on intermediate execution results. To minimize the weighted sum of job completion latencies, this paper models partially revealed agent workflows using dynamic workflow graphs and formulates an online scheduling problem that jointly optimizes computation placement, wireless resource block allocation, and edge computing resource allocation. To address the uncertainty of future workflow evolution, we first transform the weighted completion time objective into an equivalent per-slot holding cost and characterize the optimal policy through a Bellman equation. We then construct a tractable look-ahead cost-to-go surrogate based on the revealed workflow and the estimated remaining latencies of active jobs. The proposed scheduling algorithm leverages the surrogate to determine computation placement and uses the resulting operation criticality to allocate wireless and edge computing resources online. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the benchmark schemes across diverse scenarios.

title: Energy-Efficient Timely Relevant IoT Data Retrieval with Wireless Memory Approximation
summary: Collecting relevant data from Internet of Things devices under freshness and energy constraints is a key challenge in 6G edge networks. A lightweight neural network on the device filters irrelevant observations, but storing it in dynamic random access memory consumes refresh energy during standby. This letter proposes a pull-based framework where an edge server remotely activates and approximates memory and jointly selects the activation timing, refresh period, model size, and transmission threshold. We derive the expected freshness and energy over erasure channels in closed form and show that the scheme consumes less energy than an always-on baseline under the same freshness constraint.

title: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum
summary: A quantum computer could recover the key of any Ethereum account whose public key appears on chain. We prove that no sidechain or bridge that leaves Ethereum's rules unchanged can protect such accounts: their funds must move into a contract whose release condition relies only on quantum-safe primitives. We design \emph{PQ-Vault}, a custody system for unmodified Ethereum combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain whose checkpoints carry compact certificates, and an optimistic dispute protocol. We give the first security proof of compact certificates against quantum attackers and a matching attack: with classically chosen parameters, the guarantee falls from 128 to about 60 bits, and a simple rule restores it. We show that a common seed-update rule in hash-chain proof of stake lets an attacker steer chosen slots and profit from splitting its stake, and give an election whose steering gain and inclusion delay are provably bounded against quantum attackers. Since compressing certificates with a pairing-based SNARK breaks quantum security, we use fraud proofs that need a single signature check. For 65,536 validators, a certificate is 0.8 MB, 260 times smaller than all signatures, and verifies in about 20 ms; the vault accepts a checkpoint for about 420,000 gas.

title: Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions
summary: Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart. We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms. Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.

title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
summary: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond
summary: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, among the crashes discovered by 5uGUE, MediaTek has confirmed two new high-severity vulnerabilities, with one CVE assigned (CVE-2026-20525), while UNISOC confirmed seven crashes. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our evaluations, 5uGUE finds an average of 6.4 novel crashes and 1.6 unique crashes. In a nutshell, 5uGUE highlights that LLM agents are capable to operate effectively beyond software-in-the-loop settings, extending autonomous vulnerability discovery to the proprietary, hardware-bound systems that affect billions of end-user devices across multiple wireless protocols.

title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
summary: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.

title: Koala: Non-disruptive Reconfiguration for Long-running Stateful Dataflows
summary: Stateful dataflow systems must decide where state lives relative to the tasks that process it. For long-running applications that require frequent reconfiguration due to changes in resource allocation, partitioning, or task placement, this design choice presents a core trade-off between adaptability and performance. Co-locating state with computation ensures low latency at steady state but makes reconfiguration disruptive, as any change forces state migration. On the other hand, keeping state in an external store makes reconfiguration seamless, but incurs overhead on every access. We present Koala, a reconfiguration protocol for distributed dataflow systems that retains the operational performance of embedded-state architectures while matching the disruption-free adaptability of external-state designs. Unlike prior protocols which relocate all state regardless of whether it will soon be accessed, Koala migrates state in a fine-grained, lazy manner. To achieve that, it employs a lightweight ownership transfer mechanism that safely decouples event routing from state location. We implement Koala in a new streaming dataflow system and evaluate it on real-world and synthetic benchmarks. When compared with the state-of-the-art protocol DRRS, Koala consumes backlog up to 23x faster and transfers 8.7x less state on average during reconfiguration.

title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
summary: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $Δ$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrtΔ,n^2/Δ\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.

title: Engineering Low-Latency, High-Throughput Quantum Decoders on NVIDIA GPUs
summary: We design and optimize a quantum error correction (QEC) decoder for NVIDIA GPUs, combining Relay belief propagation, a state-of-the-art message-passing algorithm, with order-zero ordered statistics post-processing. Our implementation uses CUDA Graphs to control GPU execution, stops updates for converged samples, and collects unresolved samples in queues for post-processing. We optimize sparse traversal through coalesced message accesses, prefetching, and register reuse, and accelerate binary post-processing with warp-level collectives. In addition, mixed FP16-FP32 arithmetic and INT8 quantization reduce message storage and traffic while retaining accuracy using accumulators at higher precision. We evaluate surface, hypergraph product, and bivariate bicycle code workloads on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 data-center GPUs and a commodity RTX 5080. On the bivariate bicycle code at error probability 0.003, INT8 halves amortized decoding time relative to independently tuned FP32 with a negligible logical error rate increase on RTX 5080. With independent syndrome batches submitted back-to-back to concurrent decoder instances, RTX 5080 delivers 91% of GH200's highest measured throughput with an 8.9x shorter median submission-to-correction latency. The combination of performance optimization, mixed precision, INT8 quantization, and concurrent decoder instances opens a path toward QEC decoder clusters built from commodity GPUs.

title: Agent AI Zarządzający Siecią Open RAN Zorientowana na Użytkownika
summary: Jednym z najważniejszych wyzwań związanych z implementacją sieci Open RAN o architekturze zorientowanej na użytkownika jest odpowiednie formowanie tzw. klastrów obsługujących. Problem ten może być efektywnie rozwiązany za pomocą zaproponowanego Agenta AI bazującego na modelu językowym. Wyniki symulacji pokazały, że zaproponowane rozwiązanie pozwala na ponad 2-krotne zwiększenie mediany rozkładu przepływności użytkowników względem standardowej architektury zorientowanej na sieć.

title: SAT Sampling at Scale via GPU-based Boolean Constraint Propagation
summary: Constrained-random verification tests hardware designs by sampling solutions of Boolean formulas. Existing samplers largely follow one of two approaches: CPU-based SAT samplers (e.g., CMSGen), which remain effective even at rare targets but offer limited throughput, and GPU-based gradient samplers, which achieve high throughput at high-probability targets but collapse at rare ones. We introduce Gpap-S, the first GPU sampler built on Boolean constraint propagation (BCP). At its core is Gpap, a new GPU engine for BCP that efficiently propagates many independent partial assignments concurrently on a shared Boolean formula. This capability allows Gpap-S to combine the rare-target robustness of SAT-based sampling with the throughput of GPU parallelism by exploring thousands of decide-and-propagate trajectories simultaneously. On the benchmark families used to evaluate prior GPU gradient samplers, Gpap-S is 2.2-18.7x faster at the high-probability targets considered in those evaluations. At rare targets, where those samplers often fail to generate any samples, Gpap-S achieves a geometric-mean speedup of roughly two orders of magnitude. Across all benchmarks, Gpap-S is also 83.4-1,571x faster than the CPU-based CMSGen. This throughput does not come at the expense of sample quality: under Barbarik, the statistical tester used to evaluate CMSGen, Gpap-S is accepted on every instance we test, as is CMSGen. We release Gpap as a reusable GPU library for high-throughput BCP.

title: GPU-Accelerated Construction of the Gabriel Graph: Parallelization Strategies and Applications to Large-Margin Classification and Graph-Based Clustering
summary: The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph widely used in computational geometry and geometric machine learning, underlying large-margin classifiers and, as we show in this work, density-aware clustering methods. Its construction, however, has cubic time complexity $O(N^3)$ in the naive formulation, which severely limits its use on datasets beyond a few thousand samples. This paper presents a set of GPU parallelization strategies, implemented in CUDA, that make Gabriel graph construction practical at scale. We introduce (i) an implicit closed-form mapping from a linear thread index to the corresponding vertex pair $(i,j)$, which removes the need for an explicit $O(N^2)$ adjacency structure and lets every thread locate its pair in constant time and constant memory; (ii) a two-pass, bitmask-based, atomically-compacted edge-list construction that produces a dense edge array proportional only to the number of edges actually found; and (iii) a thread-coarsening strategy in which each thread evaluates several candidate pairs, trading launch and scheduling overhead against load balance. We evaluate these strategies on the acceleration of a Gabriel-graph-based large-margin classifier (NN-clas) and on a novel Gabriel-graph clustering algorithm that identifies connected components on a residual graph and performs GPU-parallel Union-Find with hierarchical edge-based merging. On 14 public benchmark datasets, the GPU implementation reduces Gabriel graph construction time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude relative to a sequential CPU baseline (up to 8484x), without loss of classification accuracy, and the proposed clustering method is statistically competitive with DBSCAN on the topological validity index Dunn while eliminating the need for an explicit density radius parameter.

title: Weight Placement Is Not Enough: Synchronization in Multi-Node CPU Decoding of Ternary LLMs
summary: Ternary LLMs read only a few gigabytes per decoded token, yet on dual-socket servers with four NUMA nodes the fastest ternary runtime we found uses less than half of the memory bandwidth. Placing each weight on the node of the thread that reads it is necessary but not enough: in a decode engine with node-local weights that reuses ik_llama's kernels, threads on two generations of Xeon servers still spend 20-48% of each token waiting at synchronization points. Per-thread barrier traces show that most of the wait is for the slowest threads of each node; the barriers' own latency (microseconds each, but up to 12% of the token for the smallest model) and serial per-node work are smaller parts. On identical kernels, a Megatron-style column split beats a row-owned split without cross-node reductions in every configuration we measured, and isolating the number of barriers shows that most of its gain comes from its threads waiting less for each other and for their node leaders, and only a minority from having fewer barriers. Where decoding is DRAM-bound, the resulting engine is 1.5-2.1x faster than ik_llama with all cores and 1.5-1.9x faster than ik_llama at its fastest thread count (3.2x and 2.8x for a small model that runs from the L3 cache), at the same accuracy and with less energy per token.

title: Entanglement Distribution in Quantum Switch Networks: Memory Limits and Achievability
summary: We study the minimum persistent memory required to distribute a graph state through a quantum switch. Specifically, consider a central switch that assists $n$ remote users in distributing a graph state, using independently generated user-switch Bell pairs. Since Bell-pair generation is probabilistic, different links generally succeed at different times. When a Bell-pair is generated, the qubits may need to be stored in memory while waiting for other links to succeed. Recently, new protocols have been proposed to reduce this storage overhead by processing and releasing some switch qubits before all Bell links are available. However, these protocols do not characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required at each stage. Moreover, the local-cover method in the state-of-the-art Piecemaker protocol is computationally expensive for general target graphs. In this work, we characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required after any subset of users' Bell links are generated and processed. We then develop an online stabilizer-transition protocol that attains this limit, which can be implemented in polynomial time in the number of qubits $n$. Remarkably, this optimal protocol can provide substantial memory reductions over existing heuristic approaches. In particular, for the path graph $P_n$ over $n$ users, Piecemaker protocol requires at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ qubits of peak persistent memory for \textit{every Bell-links generation order}, whereas under the order $(1,2,\ldots,n)$, our protocol requires only one persistent switch qubit. Finally, the same stabilizer-transition framework also provides a direct forward construction for sequential graph-state generation using the minimum number of quantum emitters, equal to the maximum of the height function.

title: The Token-Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token
summary: Energy-efficient deployment of large language models requires understanding how model architecture, hardware, and serving settings shape energy per generated token. We introduce the Token-Energy Law, a compact, interpretable model of GPU-board energy per output token for dense, full-history decoding. It relates token energy to two core dimensions: active bytes and realized decode time. Active bytes describe logical byte demand per output, separating dense weights shared within a decode iteration from private key--value (KV) histories read and updated for each request. Realized decode time is the elapsed decode duration divided by the number of output tokens produced. We combine the two byte coordinates and time in a common affine form, with coefficients calibrated for each model and hardware/runtime configuration. This formulation explains how batching amortizes shared-weight work, longer attended histories increase private KV demand, and throughput determines the time-associated cost per output. Our experiments cover three models under BF16 decoding on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, including two-GPU tensor parallelism on Hopper. Using fixed coefficients and observed decode time, held-out condition-mean energy estimates differ from measurements by at most 3.73%.

title: Discount Yourself: Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip for Decentralised Learning under Client Outages
summary: Decentralised federated learning (DFL) trains personalised models on devices that average with their neighbours rather than with a central server. Real devices, however, are often offline for hours or days, and a client returning from an outage can recover only by aggregating the models its neighbourhood holds. We observe that the stalest of these models is usually the client's own, a case that existing staleness-aware rules, which discount only the models a client receives, do not address. We formalise aggregation after an outage as estimating the state of a fully available network and derive three principles. First, the receiver must be discounted like any neighbour. Every rule that weights it at least as much as each neighbour has an error that grows without bound with the outage, whereas discounting all candidates by relative staleness keeps the error bounded. Second, staleness must be measured as inherited lag rather than age, since local training resets a model's age but not the lag it absorbed from stale neighbours. We introduce the effective lag, which tracks this quantity at the cost of one scalar per message. Third, the discount must be steep, because absorbed lag persists in every later round. These principles define Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip (SFG), a family of drop-in aggregation rules with the communication and computation of decentralised federated averaging, whose guarantees hold for the stale receiver itself. On three image benchmarks and eight outage processes, including real smartphone availability traces, the lag-based members SFG-L and SFG-Cut consistently outperform decentralised federated averaging and recent age-of-information rules, and ablations show that each principle is necessary. The analysis also explains why tuned limited merging from gossip learning is effective.

title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
summary: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

title: ORCA: Onboard Reflective Collaborative Agents for Reliable Task Offloading in LEO Satellite Networks
summary: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites increasingly perform time-critical onboard processing, yet heterogeneous computing capabilities, rapidly changing inter-satellite links (ISLs) and uncertain neighbor behavior make decentralized task offloading difficult under partial observations. This paper presents ORCA, an architecture of Onboard Reflective Collaborative Agents for autonomous onboard task offloading. ORCA organizes offloading decisions into a four-Agent \emph{Perceive}$\rightarrow$\emph{Reason}$\rightarrow$ \emph{Act}$\rightarrow$\emph{Learn} loop. It aims to improve efficiency and reliability in dynamic, heterogeneous, and unreliable LEO satellite networks. The simulation results of a heterogeneous 60-satellite Walker-delta constellation demonstrates that ORCA delivers competitive system efficiency in cooperative settings while achieving superior task-success robustness and offloading reliability under previously unseen malicious node behavior, indicating that outcome-grounded reflection can improve the reliability of decentralized onboard offloading without centralized runtime coordination.

title: Budgeted Admission from Timestamped Capacity Records in Shared Clusters
summary: A cluster admission gate can receive a capacity record that no longer matches current schedulability. We study one exogenous binary schedulability unit under a bound on the joint probability of admission and unavailability. For a symmetric Markov state, we derive the stationary admission frontier for a fixed observation delay and apply finite likelihood allocation to a delay-tagged delivered record. A one-sided exact binomial endpoint calibrates each fitted policy, and exact enumeration confirms the per-policy confidence target in every tested parameter cell. A separate deterministic guard charges every unresolved admission against the realized allowance and bounds unavailable-state admissions at every prefix under truthful outcome feedback. An executable admission procedure composes the allocation and guard. The controlled system binds source sampling, NATS delivery, randomized admission, Kubernetes objects, and API-derived outcomes in one append-only record. Independent audit finds no missing event, identity mismatch, or state mismatch in the completed functional block. A separate CPU request-accounting check preserves Job and Pod identity across an unschedulable-to-complete transition.

title: RPolyPlan: A Unified Global Floorplanning and Legalization Framework for Rectilinear Soft Modules
summary: Floorplanning with rectilinear soft modules improves area utilization and wirelength by allowing modules to adapt to rectilinear polygon (RPoly) shapes. Existing methods typically construct rectilinear polygons through incremental refinement after obtaining a rectangular global solution, which confines polygon exploration to the neighborhood induced by the initial floorplan. This paper presents RPolyPlan, a unified framework for outline-free and fixed-outline floorplanning that directly incorporates continuously deformable rectilinear polygons into global floorplanning. To enable direct polygon optimization, we introduce a structured continuous representation and a differentiable polygon shaping model that dynamically optimizes rectilinear module shapes based on overlaps, making continuous shape optimization feasible for gradient-based global floorplanning. An augmented Lagrangian formulation robustly handles the coupled inequality constraints, provides theoretical convergence guarantees, and reduces dependence on manual penalty-parameter tuning. During legalization, minimum-cost flow and rectangular decomposition determine the target areas of subrectangles, and horizontal and vertical constraint graphs encode their geometric relations. The resulting convex legalization formulation satisfies the area, shape, separation, connectivity, and outline constraints while minimizing either the chip area or the displacement from the global floorplanning solution. Experiments on the GSRC, MCNC, and ICCAD 2023 contest benchmarks demonstrate that RPolyPlan reduces HPWL over the evaluated state-of-the-art methods by 7% and 6% in fixed-outline and outline-free experiments, respectively.

title: DiffRMST: A GPU-Accelerated Fully Differentiable Rectilinear Minimum Spanning Tree Wirelength Model for Global Placement
summary: Analytical global placement requires a differentiable wirelength objective that accurately reflects routed interconnect cost. The widely used half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is efficient but overlooks the internal topology of multi-pin nets. The rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT) provides higher fidelity, but its underlying decision problem is NP-complete, and its discrete construction precludes direct use in gradient-based optimization. The rectilinear minimum spanning tree (RMST) offers a polynomial-time alternative, but remains nondifferentiable because of minimization over discrete spanning trees. To address these limitations, we present DiffRMST, a fully differentiable RMST wirelength model for analytical global placement. DiffRMST combines spatial smoothing with a log-sum-exp relaxation to define a continuous distribution over spanning trees. Based on the Kirchhoff matrix-tree theorem, the partition function and edge marginals can be computed without explicit tree enumeration, enabling a closed-form topology-aware gradient for placement optimization. For efficient integration into analytical placement, we further develop a fused forward-backward operator with parallel CPU and GPU implementations. On the ISPD2019 benchmark suite, our method reduces RMST, RSMT, and routed wirelength by an average of 5.0%, 3.2%, and 3.5%, respectively, compared with the weighted-average baseline, while maintaining acceptable runtime. Furthermore, the GPU implementation achieves an average $14.7\times$ speedup in global placement over its eight-thread CPU counterpart.

title: Agentic Communication Networks: When Agents Become Network Entities
summary: Autonomous agents are moving from application-layer components to active participants in networked systems. They not only generate traffic but also perceive context, express intent, invoke services, coordinate with other agents, and act under task, policy, and resource constraints. This evolution exposes a mismatch between emerging agentic interactions and conventional endpoint- and traffic-centric network abstractions. This white paper introduces Agentic Communication Networks (ACN) as a network-centric paradigm for the time when agents become first-order network entities. At its core, ACN reshapes networking around three fundamental aspects. First, agents are represented as identifiable and governable network entities with explicit identity, authority, and lifecycle. Second, agentic services are expressed through intent, capability, context, policy, and task state, allowing the network to capture what an agent seeks to accomplish and under what conditions. Third, agentic execution becomes an explicit network concern as tasks involve multiple agents, services, tools, and distributed capabilities across heterogeneous infrastructures. Based on these shifts, the paper defines the scope, principles, architecture, and research directions of ACN, positioning it as a networking foundation for autonomous agent ecosystems.

title: Evict Early, Decode Efficiently: Lightweight Decoding Strategies for Low-Delay Sliding Window RLNC
summary: Random Linear Network Coding (RLNC), and in particular Sliding Window RLNC (SW-RLNC), is a promising approach for reliable, low-latency communication in dynamic environments such as 6G and non-terrestrial networks. While prior work has largely focused on encoder-side parameter tuning, such as the code rate and coding window size, decoder-side design remains comparatively underexplored despite its direct impact on end-to-end performance. This paper addresses decoding window management, namely the policies governing window-boundary updates, removal of obsolete packets, and delivery of recovered packets to upper layers, and shows that these policies critically shape the trade-off between computational complexity and decoding performance, particularly in-order delivery delay. We derive sufficient conditions under which packets can be safely removed from the decoding window without compromising decodability or violating in-order delivery guarantees, and, building on these conditions, propose two lightweight decoding window management schemes. Through extensive simulation-based evaluation across a range of channel conditions and code rates, we show that both schemes preserve decoding efficiency while substantially reducing decoding complexity, and that one additionally achieves a marked reduction in in-order delivery delay. These results establish decoding window management as a key design dimension for practical SW-RLNC systems.

title: KPage: Cross-Block Page Compaction for Hardware-Efficient Sparse Attention
summary: Sparse attention reduces the computational cost of long-sequence video Transformers, but three-dimensional token layouts often leave selected blocks partially occupied, wasting physical tile capacity. We present KPage, a block-sparse attention scheme that packs valid 16-row K/V pages across logical-block boundaries into large tiles directly during loading, without materializing compacted tensors in high-bandwidth memory. KPage also routes Q blocks between 64x256 and 128x128 tiles to reduce query-side padding. Exact masking and K/V-owned page packing preserve the original sparse graph in forward and backward execution. Across five representative workloads, KPage achieves 1.35x-2.06x bare forward-kernel speedup over NVIDIA Block-Sparse Attention (BSA), with a geometric mean of 1.77x. It is near parity for fully occupied blocks (1.03x) but achieves 2.29x geometric-mean speedup on 3D layouts with partial blocks. KPage reduces physical query-key pair capacity from 334.1G to 177.5G while preserving 160.6G useful interactions. Across eight layouts from open-source SSTA, STA, and VSA systems, KPage achieves 1.13x-4.25x forward and 1.02x-2.71x forward-plus-backward speedup over the strongest exact sparse baselines. With independent Q/K partitions, KPage also achieves 1.49x speedup over the strongest exact sparse baseline and 1.57x over BSA on the SVG2 Wan 14B/720p configuration. After compliance review, we will open-source KPage and submit a pull request to NVIDIA cuDNN Frontend.

title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
summary: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.

title: A Unified Framework for Image-to-3D Part Generation via Variable Granularity
summary: Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image-to-3D part generation framework that supports variable-granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross-modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter-task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole-mesh quality. The code can be found at https://github.com/Gucci233/FlexPart

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
summary: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
summary: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
summary: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent $α>1$ and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared $L_2$ approximation rate $\mathcal{O}((κ_P\log(m/δ)/m)^α)$ for two-layer networks of width $m$ and trainable proportion $P$, where $κ_P=(P/κ_1^*+(1-P)/κ_0^*)^{-1}$. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least $1-δ$. The constants $κ_0^*$ and $κ_1^*$ quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension $d$, we verify these assumptions with $α=(d+2)/(d-1)$ and $κ_0^*=4\sqrt{2}τ(d+1)/d$ for initialization scale $τ\ge1$, and $κ_1^*=1$ under ridge leverage sampling. For $d=5$ and $τ=10$, a trainable proportion of approximately $4.1\%$ captures $90\%$ of the reduction in the approximation bound from $P=0$ to $P=1$. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
summary: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments. Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: SpectralCanary: Embarrassingly Simple Low-Frequency Traces for T2I Dataset-Use Auditing
summary: Auditing whether a text-to-image (T2I) model was fine-tuned on a particular image collection is difficult: a model can absorb collection-level visual characteristics without reproducing training images. Proactive dataset-use auditing plants a shared signal in a dataset before release, then later checks whether that signal appears in a suspect model's generated outputs. Existing approaches often trade off verifiability, fidelity, robustness, and deployability. We introduce $\textbf{SpectralCanary}$, which uses a smooth low-pass mask to blend a fixed canary image into every collection image while leaving captions unchanged and requiring neither auxiliary generation nor per-image optimization. A lightweight verifier detects the transferred signal in suspect-model outputs. Across eight tests on the Pokemon dataset and three realistic data transformations, spanning two architectures families, SpectralCanary achieves the highest average per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR ($91.1\%$) and fixed threshold model-level accuracy using 30 generations ($94.8\%$) among the evaluated methods. Across five datasets spanning artistic, medical, satellite, and fashion domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary averages $92.4\%$ per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR while preserving the released images (SSIM $0.989$, LPIPS $0.022$) with a near-zero mean change FID (mean $Δ$FID $0.05$) across datasets.
